newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British Steel hit by destocking.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British Steel hit by destocking.

text.p: British Steel Plc on Monday said its pretax profit fell more than 50 percent in the first half, hit by destocking and weak underlying demand in Europe.

The company's pretax profit of 262 million pounds ($431.7 million) for the half year to September 28 fell within analysts' expected range of 250 to 280 million but was sharply lower than the 550 million it reported for the year-ago period.
As expected, the company maintained its interim dividend at 3.0 pence per share.

"Demand for our steel products in the UK was satisfactory but remained weak in mainland Europe due to continued destocking through the supply chain and weak underlying demand," chairman Brian Moffat said in a statement.
However, he told a news conference later that the company was cautiously optimistic about the mainland European steel market through the first half of 1997.
"The destocking phase in mainland Europe is ending," Moffat said, noting price increases in structural, flat and stainless steel products.
"Turning to British steel (the UK market), we see most of our operations working at full capacity with a strong order book going forward through second half 1996-97," he added.
Moffat said one note of caution was the strengthening of the pound and its impact on prices and the competitiveness of British Steel's UK customers in their export markets.
The company said it had hedged most of its contractual obligations through the end of this year to guard against currency fluctuations.
British steel's shares were little fazed by its results, firming 3/4 pence to close at 171-3/4 pence.
The company said price falls at its British-Swedish stainless steel subsidiary, Avesta Sheffield AB, in the spring and summer were particularly severe.
"Efforts to restore prices are critical to its profitability. Whilst it is still early days, conditions do look to be favouring these increases," Moffat said.
When asked whether the company might increase its stake in the unit, he replied, "We have 51 percent of the business, and at the moment, we are quite content with that."
Regarding British Steel's 703 million pounds in net cash funds at the end of the first half, he said, "We've no current intention of special dividends or share buybacks."
Moffat said the company expected its capital expenditure to rise to about 430 million pounds this year compared to some 321 million last year.
The company had capital spending of 188 million pounds in the first half, including about 43 million for its new steelmaking and casting facilities at Tuscaloosa Steel Corp in the United States.
British Steel also unveiled plans with Jindal Iron & Steel Co Ltd to build an organic coating line and roll profiling facilities in India at a cost of 29 million pounds.
"While this first venture in this geographical area is relatively modest at this stage, I believe it signals a new and significant phase in the company's development," Moffat said. ($1=.6069 Pound)
